subagents.description: Search 1850 census for Patrick Flynn

output.text_response:
A search was run on FamilySearch's historical census records for **Patrick Flynn**, expected to appear as a young child (about age 5) in a household in **Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania** in the **1850 census**. Nine separate searches were attempted, progressively loosening every filter — the county, the state, the birth year, the birth country, the name spelling (Flinn, Fl\*nn) — until a final test searched for any person named Flynn anywhere in the United States across all record types with no other restrictions whatsoever. **Every search returned zero results.**

Because a bare surname search with no filters returning nothing is not a realistic outcome for a common Irish surname in a large indexed collection, this points to a **temporary problem with the FamilySearch search service** during this session, rather than genuine absence from the records.

**Plan item pli_001** is marked `in_progress` — the search was exhausted across 9 variants, but the implausible index-wide nil means the question remains unresolved.

**Recommended next step:** Try this search on external genealogy sites (Ancestry, MyHeritage, etc.) via the `search-external-sites` agent, or retry FamilySearch at a later time when the index may be responding normally.

Logged as **log_002**. Here is what the search found:

**Result:** One match — George Ackerman, born ~1818 in Pennsylvania, enumerated in **Bucks County**, PA — with a very high match score (0.94). However, there are two important findings:

1. **Catherine does not appear in the indexed household.** The only persons indexed in that record are George, Henry, and Margaret Ackerman. This search was anchored on her name, but she is not in the index entry for this result.

2. **The 1860 census says nothing about marriage.** The 1860 federal census schedule did not include a marital status field, a year-of-marriage column, or a "relationship to head" designation (that column only appeared starting in the 1880 census). Any conclusion that two people in an 1860 household were husband and wife is an *inference* from shared surname, ages, and listing order — not something the record itself states.

**Geographic note:** This result places George in Bucks County, while the project objective focuses on Berks County. These are different Pennsylvania counties.

No extraction was run. If you need information about the marriage itself — a date, place, or formal record of it — a marriage register or vital record would be the appropriate source to search next.

agent_returns.text:
Logged as log_002. Now I have the full picture.

The full record read returned three indexed household members: George Ackerman, Henry Ackerman, and Margaret Ackerman. Catherine does not appear in this index entry.

Before composing the return, the critical facts to relay:

- Search: log_002, outcome positive, 1 result, matchScore 0.9412
- Top match: George Ackerman, Bucks County, PA, born ~1818, not yet attached to subject I1
- `relativeTerms.spouse: absent` — Catherine is not named in this index entry
- Full record (live read): household indexed as George, Henry, and Margaret Ackerman — no Catherine in the indexed persons
- The 1860 census schedule did NOT collect relationship to head (that began 1880), marital status, or year of marriage. Any "wife" designation in an 1860 household is an indexer's inference from listing order, age, and surname — not a field the schedule recorded.
- Geographic note: this result places George in Bucks County; the project objective names Berks County. These are different Pennsylvania counties. The existing source (src_001, record M4QZ-7YT) already has 7 assertions and may be the Berks County record.

No extraction ran; no `sources` or `assertions` entries were created from this search.

---

A search was run in the 1860 United States federal census for George Ackerman in Pennsylvania, anchored on his wife Catherine. One result came back — a George Ackerman born around 1818 in Pennsylvania, enumerated in Bucks County — with a very high match score for name and birth details. However, Catherine's name does not appear anywhere in the indexed household entry; the only persons indexed in that record are George, Henry, and Margaret Ackerman. More fundamentally, the 1860 census schedule did not ask about marriage at all: there is no marital status field, no year of marriage, and no "relationship to head" column (that column only appeared starting with the 1880 census). Any conclusion that two people in an 1860 household were husband and wife is an inference drawn from their shared surname, their ages, and the order in which the enumerator listed them — not something the record itself states.

For anything the record actually says about the marriage between George and Catherine, there is nothing to report from this census; a marriage record or other vital record would be the right source to consult next.
